prompt: You maintain an MIT-licensed tool and want to add a GPL-3.0-licensed library to it. What is the correct outcome, and why?
choices: You generally cannot ship the combination under MIT — GPL-3.0's copyleft obligation applies to the combined/derivative work, so the whole distributed work would have to become GPL-3.0
This is always fine, because MIT is a more permissive license and permissive licenses override any license they're combined with
This is illegal in all cases and the GPL-licensed code can never be used by anyone outside its own project
It depends only on how many lines of GPL code you use — under a certain threshold, the GPL obligation doesn't apply

prompt: What does signing a typical Contributor License Agreement (CLA) actually commit a contributor to, in the most common form?

Permanently transferring copyright ownership of the contribution to the project, identical to a full copyright-assignment agreement
Nothing legally binding — CLAs are purely symbolic and have no real legal effect
Granting the project exclusive rights so that the contributor can no longer use their own contributed code anywhere else

prompt: Under U.S. copyright's work-made-for-hire doctrine, what is the key difference in default ownership between an employee's work and an independent contractor's work?
choices: An employee's work within the scope of employment is automatically owned by the employer; a contractor's work is not automatically work-for-hire unless a written agreement says so (and even then, only for a narrow set of legally defined categories)
Both employees' and contractors' work are automatically owned by whoever pays for it, with no agreement required in either case
A contractor automatically owns everything they create, and no contract can ever change that
An employee owns their own work by default, and the employer must get a signed assignment to claim it

prompt: Which statement about software patents is accurate and consistent with this lesson?
choices: Most ordinary application code isn't patentable, and software/business-method patents face real extra scrutiny since Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank (2014), though exactly where the line falls is genuinely fact-specific and unsettled
Any code you write is automatically eligible for a patent as soon as you write it, with no further requirements
Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank made all software patents in the U.S. completely invalid going forward
Patents and copyright protect exactly the same thing, so getting a copyright on your code also gives you patent protection

prompt: Why does a non-compete clause not have a single universal enforceability answer across the United States?

Non-compete clauses are enforced identically in every U.S. state, so the jurisdiction never actually matters
Non-competes are enforceable only in California and nowhere else in the United States
Enforceability depends solely on the length of the non-compete, with no state-law variation at all
